sections.heading: Type I-A: Fire Resistive Non-combustible
paragraphs: Commonly found in high-rise buildings and Group I occupancies

sections.heading: Type I-B: Fire Resistive Non-Combustible
paragraphs: Commonly found in mid-rise office & Group R buildings

sections.heading: Type II-A: Protected Non-Combustible
paragraphs: Commonly found in newer school buildings

sections.heading: Type II-B: Unprotected Non-Combustible
paragraphs: Most common type of non-combustible construction used in commercial buildings.
Building constructed of non-combustible materials but these materials have no fire resistance.

sections.heading: Type III-A: Protected Combustible
paragraphs: Also known as "ordinary" construction with brick or block walls and a wooden roof or floor assembly which is 1 hour fire protected.

sections.heading: Type III-B: Unprotected Combustible
paragraphs: Also known as "ordinary" construction; has brick or block walls with a wooden roof or floor assembly which is not protected against fire. These buildings are frequently found in "warehouse" districts of older cities.
No fire resistance for structural frame, floors, ceilings, or roofs.

sections.heading: Type IV: Heavy Timber
paragraphs: Also known as "mill" construction; to qualify all wooden members must have a minimum nominal dimension of 8 inches.
1 Hr. Structural Frame or Heavy Timber

sections.heading: Type V-A: Protected Wood Frame
paragraphs: Commonly used in the construction of newer apartment buildings; there is no exposed wood visible.

sections.heading: Type V-B: Unprotected Wood Frame
paragraphs: Examples of Type V-B construction are single family homes and garages.
They often have exposed wood so there is no fire resistance.
* Note exceptions in the building code for fire resistance ratings of exterior walls and opening protection.
